planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and keep the root zone consistently moist.

directions: Souliea vaginata is a little-grown Ranunculaceae relative of Actaea and Cimicifuga, native to cool montane forests of western China, forming a low clump of glossy, compound, dark-green leaflets. In spring it sends up short spikes of unusual purple-brown, cup-shaped flowers held just above the foliage, followed later by inflated, papery seed pods that add a second season of interest. It prefers the same cool, humus-rich, evenly moist woodland conditions favored by hepaticas and epimediums, and resents hot, dry summer exposure. A curiosity for specialist shade gardeners building a collection of unusual Asian woodland genera.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions or container stock in fall with the crown just below the soil surface, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: Paeonia obovata is a true forest-dwelling peony from Japan, Korea, and China, unlike most garden peonies which demand full sun. It produces soft blue-green, rounded leaflets and single, cupped white to soft pink flowers with prominent golden stamens in mid to late spring, followed by striking seed pods that split open to reveal glossy blue-black fertile seeds beside bright red infertile ones. It thrives in the dappled light beneath deciduous trees where full-sun peonies would fail, and its foliage often takes on attractive purple-red fall tones. Give it rich, well-drained woodland soil and avoid disturbing the crown once established, as peonies resent transplanting.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in early spring.

directions: Chloranthus serratus is an East Asian woodland perennial in the ancient, primitive Chloranthaceae family, forming neat whorls of glossy, serrated, deep-green leaves on upright stems. In mid to late spring it produces small spikes of unusual, fragrant, brush-like white flowers lacking true petals, composed instead of showy stamens, an intriguing structure reflecting the plant's evolutionary distinctiveness. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form a tidy, low colony in consistently moist, cool woodland shade, going dormant by late summer in hot climates. A distinctive textural companion for hostas, epimediums, and other refined shade perennials in a collector's woodland garden.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Heloniopsis orientalis is an evergreen Japanese and Korean woodland perennial in the Melanthiaceae family, forming a low rosette of strap-shaped, leathery, dark-green leaves reminiscent of a small Liriope. In early spring, before most woodland perennials have emerged, it sends up short, sturdy stems topped with nodding clusters of star-shaped, pink to rose-purple flowers with prominent stamens, providing welcome early color in the shade garden. After flowering, small plantlets sometimes form at the leaf tips, a curious means of vegetative propagation. It prefers the cool, humus-rich, evenly moist conditions of a mossy woodland floor and makes an attractive, long-lived evergreen edging plant for a shaded rock garden or path.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Anemone flaccida is a spreading Japanese woodland anemone that forms an attractive, slowly creeping carpet of deeply lobed, softly toothed, glossy green leaves beneath deciduous trees. In mid spring it bears open, five- to seven-petaled white to pale pink flowers with a central boss of yellow stamens, held just above the foliage in loose drifts. Unlike many spring ephemerals it retains attractive foliage well into summer in consistently moist shade before going dormant. It spreads gently by rhizome to naturalize into a low, weed-suppressing groundcover, making a graceful companion for hostas, ferns, and epimediums in a woodland setting.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall or early spring, 1-2 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Convallaria keiskei is the East Asian counterpart to the familiar European lily of the valley, native to Japan, Korea, and far-eastern Russia, and is considered by some taxonomists a variety of Convallaria majalis but is distinguished by generally broader leaves and slightly later, often larger, intensely fragrant white bell-shaped flowers in late spring. Like its European relative it spreads by rhizome to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under deciduous trees and shrubs, tolerating deep shade and root competition where few flowering perennials succeed. Red berries follow the flowers in late summer, adding autumn interest, though all plant parts are toxic if ingested. A reliable, tough, long-lived groundcover for difficult shaded sites.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online
